decks.title: Nitric Acid — Part 1: Laboratory preparation and Ostwald’s process
goals: Write the equation for preparing nitric acid from potassium or sodium nitrate
Describe the all-glass apparatus and explain the precautions taken
Explain why concentrated nitric acid often looks yellow
Write the equations, with conditions, for Ostwald’s process

slides.heading: Aqua fortis: strong water
slides.body_md: Part 1 — Nitric acid, HNO₃, was once called **aqua fortis** (strong water) because it attacks most metals. It is a **strong acid** and a **strong oxidising agent**, and it is made in huge amounts for **fertilisers** and **explosives**.

rows: Fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate, explosives, dyes

visual.alt: Table of the formula, appearance and uses of nitric acid

slides.narration: Namaste! Nitric acid was once called strong water, because it dissolves most metals. It is a strong acid, and also a powerful oxidising agent. Factories make it in enormous quantities, mainly to turn into fertilisers such as ammonium nitrate, and also for explosives and dyes. In this part we prepare it in the laboratory and see how it is made on a large scale.

slides.heading: Laboratory preparation
slides.body_md:
**Potassium nitrate** (or sodium nitrate) is heated gently with **concentrated sulphuric acid**. Sulphuric acid is **less volatile** (higher boiling) than nitric acid, so it drives the more volatile nitric acid out as vapour, which is then condensed.

With sodium nitrate: NaNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HNO₃.

visual.alt: Equation: potassium nitrate plus sulphuric acid gives potassium hydrogen sulphate plus nitric acid
visual.caption: Below 200 °C

slides.narration: In the laboratory, potassium nitrate is warmed with concentrated sulphuric acid. Sulphuric acid has a much higher boiling point than nitric acid, so the nitric acid formed escapes as a vapour and can be condensed. The other product is potassium hydrogen sulphate. Sodium nitrate works in exactly the same way, giving sodium hydrogen sulphate.

slides.heading: An all-glass apparatus
slides.body_md:
- A **glass retort** with a **glass stopper** holds the mixture.
- The retort neck leads into a **receiver** kept **cold** with running water.
- **No cork or rubber**: nitric acid vapour **attacks** them.
- Heat **gently**, keeping the temperature **below 200 °C**.

visual.alt: All-glass apparatus for preparing nitric acid: a stoppered glass retort of potassium nitrate and concentrated sulphuric acid heated gently, its neck leading into a receiver cooled by water

slides.narration: The whole apparatus is made of glass. The mixture is heated in a glass retort closed with a glass stopper, and its long neck leads into a receiver flask cooled by cold water. Nitric acid vapour is so corrosive that it attacks cork and rubber, so neither is used anywhere. The vapour condenses in the cold receiver as a slightly yellow liquid.

slides.heading: Why keep the temperature below 200 °C?
slides.body_md:
At higher temperatures the acid salt reacts further, which would need much more heat:

KNO₃ + KHSO₄ → K₂SO₄ + HNO₃ (needs a high temperature)

We avoid this because:

rows: Strong heat breaks it down into nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen
The retort could break at very high temperatures
Potassium sulphate forms a hard crust that is difficult to remove
More heat gives little extra acid

visual.alt: Table of four reasons for keeping the temperature below two hundred degrees Celsius

slides.narration: The mixture is heated gently, below two hundred degrees Celsius. At a higher temperature, the acid salt left behind would react with more nitrate, but that needs strong heating. Strong heat would decompose some of the nitric acid, could crack the glass retort, would leave a hard crust of potassium sulphate that is difficult to remove, and would waste fuel.

slides.heading: Worked example: how much acid?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** What mass of nitric acid can be obtained from 50.5 g of potassium nitrate, heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid below 200 °C? (K = 39, N = 14, O = 16, H = 1)

**Step 1.** KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃: 1 mole KNO₃ gives 1 mole HNO₃.

**Step 2.** KNO₃ = 39 + 14 + 48 = 101; moles = 50.5 ÷ 101 = 0.5.

**Step 3.** HNO₃ = 1 + 14 + 48 = 63; mass = 0.5 × 63 = **31.5 g**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 50.5 grams of potassium nitrate to 31.5 grams of nitric acid

slides.narration: The equation shows one unit of potassium nitrate giving one unit of nitric acid. The molar mass of potassium nitrate is one hundred and one, so fifty point five grams is half a mole. Half a mole of nitric acid, whose molar mass is sixty three, has a mass of thirty one point five grams.

slides.heading: Why the acid looks yellow
slides.body_md:
Nitric acid **decomposes** slightly on heating or in **sunlight**. The **reddish-brown nitrogen dioxide** formed dissolves in the acid and makes it **yellow**. It is stored in **dark brown bottles**.

The yellow colour can be removed by **bubbling dry air** (or carbon dioxide) through the **warm** acid, which sweeps out the NO₂, or by **adding water**, which converts the dissolved NO₂ into nitric acid.

visual.alt: Equation: four nitric acid gives four nitrogen dioxide plus two water plus oxygen
visual.caption: Decomposition by heat or light

slides.narration: Pure nitric acid is colourless, but the acid in the laboratory often looks yellow. Heat and sunlight break a little of it down into nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen. The reddish brown nitrogen dioxide dissolves in the acid and colours it yellow. That is why nitric acid is kept in brown bottles. Blowing dry air through the warm acid removes the colour.

slides.heading: Ostwald’s process: step 1
slides.body_md: **Dry ammonia** and **air** (about **1 : 10** by volume) are passed over a **platinum gauze** catalyst at about **800 °C**. Ammonia is oxidised to **nitric oxide**. The reaction is **exothermic**, so once started it keeps the gauze **red-hot** without outside heating.

visual.alt: Equation: four ammonia plus five oxygen gives four nitric oxide plus six water
visual.caption: Platinum gauze, about 800 °C

slides.narration: Industry makes nitric acid by Ostwald’s process. Dry ammonia mixed with about ten times its volume of air is passed over a platinum gauze heated to about eight hundred degrees Celsius. The ammonia is oxidised to nitric oxide and steam. The reaction gives out heat, so after it starts, the gauze stays red hot on its own.

slides.heading: Ostwald’s process: steps 2 and 3
slides.body_md:
**Step 2.** On cooling, nitric oxide combines with more oxygen to give **nitrogen dioxide**: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂.

**Step 3.** Nitrogen dioxide is **absorbed in water** in the presence of **excess air** to give nitric acid: 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃.

Overall, one molecule of NH₃ gives one molecule of HNO₃.

visual.alt: Flow of the three steps of Ostwald’s process from ammonia and air to nitric acid

slides.narration: The nitric oxide is cooled, and it combines with more oxygen from the air to form reddish brown nitrogen dioxide. This gas is then dissolved in water while extra air is supplied, which gives nitric acid. Follow the nitrogen atom: one ammonia molecule ends up as one nitric acid molecule.

slides.heading: Worked example: acid from ammonia
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** In Ostwald’s process, what mass of nitric acid can be made from 6.8 g of ammonia, assuming complete conversion? (N = 14, H = 1, O = 16)

**Step 1.** Follow the nitrogen: 4NH₃ → 4NO → 4NO₂ → 4HNO₃, so 1 mole NH₃ gives 1 mole HNO₃.

**Step 2.** NH₃ = 17; moles = 6.8 ÷ 17 = 0.4.

**Step 3.** Mass of HNO₃ = 0.4 × 63 = **25.2 g**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 6.8 grams of ammonia to 25.2 grams of nitric acid

slides.narration: Look at the three equations together. Four ammonia molecules give four nitric oxide, then four nitrogen dioxide, then four nitric acid, so the ratio is one to one. Six point eight grams of ammonia is zero point four mole, since its molar mass is seventeen. Zero point four mole of nitric acid has a mass of twenty five point two grams.

slides.heading: Physical properties
slides.body_md: Pure nitric acid is a **colourless, fuming** liquid with a **choking smell**, **heavier than water**, and it **mixes with water in all proportions**. It is **corrosive**: it stains skin **yellow** and burns it, so it is handled with great care.

rows: Colourless when pure; yellow when it holds dissolved NO₂
Mixes with water in all proportions

visual.alt: Table of the physical properties of nitric acid

slides.narration: Pure nitric acid is a colourless liquid that fumes in moist air and has a choking smell. It is heavier than water and mixes with it in any amount. It is very corrosive: a drop on the skin burns it and leaves a yellow stain, so it must always be handled with care.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Laboratory: KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃, heated below 200 °C.
All-glass apparatus with a cooled receiver; no cork or rubber.
Yellow colour: dissolved NO₂ from decomposition; store in brown bottles.

visual.alt: Summary table comparing the laboratory preparation and Ostwald’s process

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. In the laboratory, potassium nitrate is heated gently with concentrated sulphuric acid in an all glass apparatus, below two hundred degrees Celsius. The acid looks yellow because of dissolved nitrogen dioxide. In Ostwald’s process, ammonia is oxidised over hot platinum to nitric oxide, which becomes nitrogen dioxide and then nitric acid.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write KHSO₄ (not K₂SO₄) as the product below 200 °C.
Give two reasons for “all-glass”: the vapour attacks cork and rubber.
Quote conditions with each Ostwald equation: platinum, about 800 °C, ammonia to air 1 : 10.
Plant details are not needed: equations with conditions are enough.

rows: Water and oxygen (air) are both needed

visual.alt: Table of three common slips in Part 1 and their fixes

slides.narration: Some tips. Below two hundred degrees Celsius the product is potassium hydrogen sulphate, so do not write potassium sulphate. Explain the all glass apparatus by saying that the vapour attacks cork and rubber. In Ostwald’s process, the catalyst is platinum, not iron, and the last step needs both water and oxygen.

decks.title: Nitric Acid — Part 2: Oxidising and acidic properties, and tests
goals: Explain why nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent
Write equations for concentrated and dilute nitric acid with copper, and for the concentrated acid with carbon and sulphur
Explain why only very dilute nitric acid gives hydrogen, and with which metals
Write equations for nitric acid with bases, carbonates, hydrogen carbonates and sulphites, and describe tests for the acid

slides.heading: Two personalities
slides.body_md: Part 2 — Nitric acid behaves both as an **acid** (it gives H⁺ ions) and as an **oxidising agent** (it gives oxygen). Which one wins depends on the **concentration** and on what it meets.

rows: A nitrate or oxide, water and NO₂ or NO
A nitrate, water (and CO₂ or SO₂)
Only very dilute acid with Mg or Mn

visual.alt: Table of the two kinds of behaviour of nitric acid with typical reactions and products

slides.narration: Nitric acid has two personalities. As an acid, it gives hydrogen ions and reacts with bases and carbonates like any other acid. As an oxidising agent, it gives oxygen, which attacks metals and non metals, and nitrogen dioxide or nitric oxide comes off. The concentration of the acid decides which behaviour we see.

slides.heading: Why it oxidises
slides.body_md:
Nitric acid **decomposes to give oxygen**, which oxidises the substance it meets:

- **Concentrated acid:** 2HNO₃ → H₂O + 2NO₂ + [O], one atom of oxygen for every two molecules of acid
- **Dilute acid:** 2HNO₃ → H₂O + 2NO + 3[O], three atoms of oxygen for every two molecules

The **reddish-brown NO₂** (from concentrated acid) or **colourless NO** (from dilute acid) is the sign of oxidation.

visual.alt: Table of the gases given by concentrated and dilute nitric acid when they act as oxidising agents

slides.narration: Nitric acid oxidises because it easily breaks down and releases oxygen. Concentrated acid releases oxygen and forms reddish brown nitrogen dioxide. Dilute acid releases more oxygen per molecule and forms colourless nitric oxide. So the colour of the gas tells us whether concentrated or dilute acid has reacted.

slides.heading: Copper and concentrated nitric acid
slides.body_md: Copper does **not** give hydrogen with dilute HCl or H₂SO₄, but nitric acid **oxidises** it. With **concentrated** acid: **reddish-brown fumes** of NO₂, and the solution turns **green**, becoming **blue** on dilution (copper nitrate).

visual.alt: Equation: copper plus four nitric acid gives copper nitrate plus two water plus two nitrogen dioxide
visual.caption: Copper with concentrated nitric acid

slides.narration: Copper sits below hydrogen in the activity series, so ordinary dilute acids do not attack it. Nitric acid is different, because it is an oxidising agent. With the concentrated acid, copper turnings dissolve quickly, thick reddish brown fumes of nitrogen dioxide pour out, and the solution turns green, then blue when water is added.

slides.heading: Quick check: copper and concentrated acid
slides.body_md: Name the gas given off when copper meets concentrated nitric acid.
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about the colour of the fumes when concentrated nitric acid oxidises copper.

slides.heading: Copper and dilute nitric acid
slides.body_md: With **moderately dilute** acid (about 1 : 1 with water) copper gives **nitric oxide**, which is **colourless** but turns **reddish brown** at the mouth of the tube as it meets air: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂.

rows: Colourless NO, brown at the mouth

visual.alt: Table comparing the reactions of copper with concentrated and dilute nitric acid

slides.narration: With dilute nitric acid, copper dissolves more slowly and the solution turns blue. The gas formed inside the tube is nitric oxide, which is colourless. As it reaches the open mouth of the tube, it meets the oxygen of the air and turns into reddish brown nitrogen dioxide. Learn both equations: four acid for every copper with the concentrated acid, eight acid for three copper with the dilute.

slides.heading: Worked example: volume of nitrogen dioxide
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** 3.175 g of copper dissolves in excess concentrated nitric acid. Find the volume of nitrogen dioxide at STP. (Cu = 63.5; molar volume 22.4 L)

**Step 1.** Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂: 1 mole Cu gives 2 moles NO₂.

**Step 2.** Moles of Cu = 3.175 ÷ 63.5 = 0.05.

**Step 3.** Moles of NO₂ = 2 × 0.05 = 0.1; volume = 0.1 × 22.4 = **2.24 L**.

visual.alt: Table of the steps from 3.175 grams of copper to 2.24 litres of nitrogen dioxide

slides.narration: One unit of copper gives two units of nitrogen dioxide with the concentrated acid. Three point one seven five grams of copper is zero point zero five mole, because the molar mass of copper is sixty three point five. Twice that is zero point one mole of gas, which occupies two point two four litres at standard conditions.

slides.heading: Carbon and sulphur
slides.body_md: **Hot concentrated** nitric acid oxidises **non-metals** to their highest oxides or oxyacids, giving reddish-brown NO₂:

visual.alt: Table of the oxidation of carbon and sulphur by hot concentrated nitric acid

slides.narration: Hot concentrated nitric acid also oxidises non metals. Powdered charcoal is oxidised to carbon dioxide, and sulphur is oxidised all the way to sulphuric acid. In both reactions, reddish brown nitrogen dioxide is given off and water is formed. Notice that carbon needs four molecules of acid and sulphur needs six.

slides.body_md: Predict the products when hot concentrated nitric acid oxidises carbon.
slides.narration: Quick check. What does carbon become when it is oxidised, and which gas comes from the acid?

slides.heading: Hydrogen only from very dilute acid
slides.body_md:
Most metals do **not** give hydrogen with nitric acid, because the acid **oxidises the hydrogen to water**. Only **very dilute** (about 1%) nitric acid gives hydrogen, and only with **magnesium** and **manganese**, which react fast enough before the hydrogen is oxidised.

Mn + 2HNO₃ → Mn(NO₃)₂ + H₂

visual.alt: Equation: magnesium plus two nitric acid gives magnesium nitrate plus hydrogen
visual.caption: Very dilute nitric acid, about 1 per cent

slides.narration: Here is a surprise. Metals such as zinc and iron give hydrogen with dilute hydrochloric acid, but not with nitric acid, because nitric acid oxidises any hydrogen to water. Only very dilute nitric acid, about one part in a hundred, gives hydrogen, and only with magnesium and manganese. These metals react so quickly that some hydrogen escapes before it can be oxidised.

slides.heading: Nitric acid as an acid
slides.body_md: Dilute nitric acid turns **blue litmus red** and reacts with bases and salts of weaker acids to form **nitrates**:

visual.alt: Table of dilute nitric acid with a basic oxide, a hydroxide, a carbonate, a hydrogen carbonate, a sulphite and a hydrogen sulphite

slides.narration: As an acid, dilute nitric acid turns blue litmus red. It neutralises basic oxides and hydroxides to give a nitrate and water. With carbonates and hydrogen carbonates it gives a nitrate, water and carbon dioxide. With sulphites and hydrogen sulphites it gives a nitrate, water and sulphur dioxide. Nitric acid has one replaceable hydrogen, so it is monobasic and forms only normal salts.

slides.heading: Worked example: matching equations to observations
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Dilute nitric acid is added to (a) black copper(II) oxide, (b) baking soda and (c) zinc oxide. State one observation for each and write the equations.

**(a)** The black solid dissolves to a **blue** solution: CuO + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.

**(b)** **Brisk effervescence** of CO₂: NaHCO₃ + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

**(c)** The white solid dissolves to a **colourless** solution: ZnO + 2HNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.

visual.alt: Table of observations and salts when dilute nitric acid reacts with copper oxide, baking soda and zinc oxide

slides.narration: Each reaction gives a nitrate. Black copper oxide dissolves to give a blue solution of copper nitrate. Baking soda fizzes as carbon dioxide escapes, leaving sodium nitrate. White zinc oxide dissolves to give a colourless solution of zinc nitrate. In every case water is also formed.

slides.heading: Tests for nitric acid
slides.body_md:
**Test 1.** Warm the acid with **copper turnings**: **reddish-brown fumes** of NO₂ and a blue-green solution.

**Test 2 (brown ring).** Add **freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate** solution, then pour **concentrated sulphuric acid** slowly down the side: a **brown ring** forms at the junction of the two layers.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. As an oxidising agent, concentrated nitric acid gives nitrogen dioxide and dilute acid gives nitric oxide, whether it meets copper or, when hot and concentrated, carbon and sulphur. As an acid, it forms nitrates with bases, carbonates and sulphites. Only very dilute acid gives hydrogen, with magnesium or manganese. Copper turnings and the brown ring test identify it.

notes.title: Study of Compounds: Nitric Acid — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Laboratory preparation
sections.body_md:
**Reactants:** potassium nitrate (or sodium nitrate) and **concentrated sulphuric acid**, heated gently.

- **Principle:** the less volatile (higher-boiling) sulphuric acid displaces the more volatile nitric acid from its salt.
- **Apparatus:** a **glass retort** with a **glass stopper**; the neck leads into a **receiver cooled by water**. The apparatus is **all glass** because nitric acid vapour **attacks cork and rubber**.
- **Temperature:** kept **below 200 °C**.

key_terms.definition_md: Apparatus with no cork or rubber parts, used because hot nitric acid vapour attacks cork and rubber.
An acid with a low boiling point that easily forms vapour, such as nitric acid.

rows: Holds the mixture; resists the acid vapour

visual.alt: Table of the parts of the apparatus for preparing nitric acid and their purposes

sections.heading: 2. Precautions, colour and physical properties
sections.body_md:
**Why below 200 °C?** At higher temperature KNO₃ + KHSO₄ → K₂SO₄ + HNO₃ would occur, but the strong heat needed would **decompose nitric acid**, may **crack the glass**, leaves a **hard crust** of K₂SO₄ and **wastes fuel**.

**Yellow colour:** heat or light decomposes some acid; the **NO₂** formed dissolves in it. Remove it by **bubbling dry air or CO₂ through the warm acid**, or by **adding water**. Store the acid in **brown bottles**.

**Physical properties:** colourless fuming liquid (pure), choking smell, heavier than water, miscible with water in all proportions, corrosive (yellow stains on skin).

key_terms.definition_md: The breakdown of nitric acid by heat or light into nitrogen dioxide, water and oxygen.

rows: The acid attacks proteins in the skin

visual.alt: Table of three observations about nitric acid and their reasons

sections.heading: 3. Ostwald’s process (equations and conditions)
sections.body_md:
**Step 1 (catalytic oxidation of ammonia):** dry ammonia and air, about **1 : 10** by volume, over **platinum gauze** at about **800 °C**. Exothermic, so the catalyst stays red-hot.

**Step 2:** nitric oxide combines with more oxygen on cooling.

**Step 3:** nitrogen dioxide is absorbed in **water** in the presence of **excess air (oxygen)**.

Overall, one NH₃ gives one HNO₃ (the nitrogen atom is carried through).

key_terms.definition_md: The industrial manufacture of nitric acid by the catalytic oxidation of ammonia over platinum.
Oxidation that takes place only in the presence of a catalyst, here platinum.

visual.alt: Table of the three steps of Ostwald’s process with conditions

sections.heading: 4. Oxidising agent: copper
sections.body_md:
Nitric acid gives **oxygen** on decomposition (conc.: 2HNO₃ → H₂O + 2NO₂ + [O]; dil.: 2HNO₃ → H₂O + 2NO + 3[O]), so it **oxidises** copper, which ordinary dilute acids cannot attack.

- **Concentrated:** reddish-brown **NO₂**; solution green, blue on dilution.
- **Dilute (about 1 : 1):** colourless **NO**, which turns reddish brown at the mouth of the tube (2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂); blue solution.

key_terms.definition_md: A substance that gives oxygen to (or removes electrons from) another substance.
NO, a colourless gas that turns reddish brown in air as it forms nitrogen dioxide.

formulas.label: Brown fumes at the mouth of the tube

visual.alt: Table of the gases formed when copper reacts with concentrated and dilute nitric acid

sections.heading: 5. Oxidising agent: carbon and sulphur
sections.body_md:
**Hot concentrated** nitric acid oxidises non-metals and gives **reddish-brown NO₂**:

- **Carbon** → carbon dioxide.
- **Sulphur** → sulphuric acid.

key_terms.definition_md: Conversion of a non-metal into its oxide or oxyacid, here by hot concentrated nitric acid.

visual.alt: Table of the products when carbon and sulphur are oxidised by concentrated nitric acid

sections.heading: 6. Acidic properties
sections.body_md:
Nitric acid is a **strong, monobasic** acid: it turns blue litmus red and forms **nitrates**.

- **Metals:** hydrogen is given only by **very dilute (about 1%)** acid with **magnesium** or **manganese**; with other metals the acid oxidises the hydrogen to water.
- **Basic oxides and hydroxides:** nitrate + water.
- **Carbonates and hydrogen carbonates:** nitrate + water + CO₂.
- **Sulphites and hydrogen sulphites:** nitrate + water + SO₂.

key_terms.definition_md: An acid with one replaceable hydrogen atom per molecule, such as nitric acid.

visual.alt: Table of four reactions showing the acidic properties of nitric acid

sections.heading: 7. Tests for nitric acid
sections.body_md:
- **Copper turnings, warmed:** reddish-brown fumes of NO₂ and a blue-green solution.
- **Brown ring test:** add **freshly prepared** iron(II) sulphate solution, then pour **conc. H₂SO₄** slowly down the side of the tube. A **brown ring** (of nitroso iron(II) sulphate, FeSO₄·NO) forms at the junction of the layers.

key_terms.definition_md: A test for nitric acid or a nitrate: a brown ring forms at the junction when concentrated sulphuric acid is layered under a mixture of the test solution and fresh iron(II) sulphate solution.

formulas.label: Nitric oxide formed in the brown ring test

rows: Brown ring at the junction of the layers

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing K₂SO₄ instead of KHSO₄ for the laboratory preparation.
- Using iron as the catalyst in Ostwald’s process (it is platinum).
- Saying dilute nitric acid gives NO₂ with copper (it gives NO).
- Writing hydrogen as a product of copper and nitric acid.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Equations (1 mark each): correct products and balancing, with “conc.” or “dil.” stated.
- Conditions (1 mark): catalyst and temperature together.
- Reasons (1 mark each): all-glass apparatus, below 200 °C, yellow colour.

questions.stem_md: The apparatus used to prepare nitric acid from potassium nitrate and concentrated sulphuric acid is made entirely of glass. The main reason is that:

options.text_md: glass conducts heat better than cork
rubber would absorb the potassium nitrate
nitric acid vapour attacks cork and rubber

questions.solution_md: Hot nitric acid vapour is highly corrosive and attacks cork and rubber, so a glass retort with a glass stopper is used — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A colourless sample of concentrated nitric acid, left in a clear glass bottle on a sunny window sill, slowly turns yellow. This is because:

options.text_md: light decomposes some of the acid, and the nitrogen dioxide formed dissolves in it
the acid absorbs moisture from the air
the acid reacts with the glass to form a yellow silicate
oxygen from the air dissolves in the acid

questions.solution_md: 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂; the reddish-brown NO₂ dissolves and colours the acid yellow — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Nitric acid is prepared by heating potassium nitrate with concentrated sulphuric acid. This works because sulphuric acid is:

options.text_md: a stronger oxidising agent than nitric acid

questions.solution_md: The higher-boiling, less volatile acid displaces the more volatile nitric acid, which distils off — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Sodium nitrate is heated gently with concentrated sulphuric acid, keeping the temperature below 200 °C. The products are:

options.text_md: sodium hydrogen sulphate and nitrogen dioxide
sodium hydrogen sulphate and nitric acid

questions.solution_md: NaNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HNO₃; the normal salt forms only at much higher temperatures — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is NOT a reason for keeping the temperature below 200 °C when preparing nitric acid in the laboratory?

options.text_md: Nitric acid would start to decompose
No nitric acid at all is formed above 200 °C
A hard crust of potassium sulphate would form

questions.solution_md: Nitric acid still forms at higher temperatures (KNO₃ + KHSO₄ → K₂SO₄ + HNO₃), but the other three effects make strong heating undesirable — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Concentrated nitric acid is stored in dark brown bottles because:

options.text_md: it absorbs moisture from the air

questions.solution_md: Brown glass keeps out light, which would decompose the acid to NO₂, water and oxygen — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In the laboratory preparation of nitric acid, the apparatus has no rubber or cork parts.

**Reason (R):** Nitric acid vapour attacks rubber and cork.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Concentrated nitric acid kept in a clear bottle in sunlight turns yellow.

**Reason (R):** Nitric acid is a weak acid.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is true (light decomposes it, giving dissolved NO₂); R is false: nitric acid is a strong acid — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Potassium sulphate is formed when potassium nitrate is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid below 200 °C.
questions.solution_md: False: below 200 °C the product is potassium hydrogen sulphate, KHSO₄.

questions.stem_md: Concentrated nitric acid is stored in ___ bottles to protect it from light.
questions.solution_md: In **brown** (dark) bottles.

questions.stem_md: In the laboratory preparation of nitric acid, the receiver is cooled with ___ so that the acid vapour condenses.
questions.solution_md: Cold running **water** (or ice) cools the receiver.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the laboratory preparation of nitric acid from sodium nitrate.

answer.model_answer_md: NaNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → NaHSO₄ + HNO₃ (below 200 °C).

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the decomposition of nitric acid by sunlight.

answer.model_answer_md: 4HNO₃ → 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: What mass of nitric acid, in grams, is obtained when 20.2 g of potassium nitrate is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid below 200 °C? (K = 39, N = 14, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{KNO3 + H2SO4 -> KHSO4 + HNO3}$: one mole of potassium nitrate gives one mole of nitric acid. Molar mass of $\ce{KNO3} = 39 + 14 + 3 \times 16 = 101$. Moles $= \dfrac{20.2}{101} = 0.2$. Molar mass of $\ce{HNO3} = 1 + 14 + 3 \times 16 = 63$. Mass of nitric acid $= 0.2 \times 63 = 12.6$, so 12.6 g.

questions.stem_md: Concentrated nitric acid in the laboratory is often yellow. (a) Explain why. (b) How can the yellow colour be removed?

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Heat or light decomposes some of the acid (4HNO₃ → 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂); the reddish-brown nitrogen dioxide dissolves in the acid and colours it yellow. (b) By bubbling dry air (or carbon dioxide) through the warm acid, which drives out the NO₂, or by adding water.

questions.solution_md: Dissolved NO₂; blow air through warm acid.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why the temperature is kept below 200 °C in the laboratory preparation of nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Any two: at higher temperatures nitric acid decomposes (giving NO₂); the glass apparatus may crack; a hard crust of potassium sulphate forms that is difficult to remove; more fuel is wasted for little extra acid.

questions.solution_md: Two reasons.

questions.stem_md: In the first step of Ostwald’s process, ammonia is oxidised to nitric oxide. The catalyst and the approximate temperature are:
questions.solution_md: 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O over platinum at about 800 °C — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In Ostwald’s process, the colourless gas leaving the platinum gauze is cooled and mixed with more air. The gas formed is:
questions.solution_md: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; nitric oxide is colourless and nitrogen dioxide is reddish brown — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The last step of Ostwald’s process, which produces nitric acid, needs:
questions.solution_md: 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the first step of Ostwald’s process, dry ammonia is mixed with air in the ratio, by volume, of about:
questions.solution_md: Ammonia and air are mixed in about 1 : 10 by volume — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In Ostwald’s process, the platinum gauze stays red-hot without outside heating once the reaction has started.

**Reason (R):** Platinum is a good conductor of electricity.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the gauze stays hot because the oxidation of ammonia is exothermic, not because platinum conducts electricity — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Platinum is the catalyst for the oxidation of ammonia in Ostwald’s process.
questions.solution_md: True: a platinum gauze at about 800 °C.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the conversion of nitrogen dioxide into nitric acid in Ostwald’s process.

answer.model_answer_md: 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: For Ostwald’s process: (a) name the catalyst and the temperature used in the first step; (b) write the balanced equations for the second and third steps; (c) explain why extra air is supplied in the third step.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Platinum gauze; about 800 °C. (b) 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃. (c) Oxygen is a reactant in the third step: without it, nitrogen dioxide and water alone would not convert all the nitrogen into nitric acid.

questions.solution_md: Pt, 800 °C; two equations; oxygen needed.

questions.stem_md: A few drops of concentrated nitric acid are poured onto copper turnings in a test tube. The gas given off is:
questions.solution_md: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂ — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Powdered charcoal is heated with concentrated nitric acid. The products are:

options.text_md: carbon monoxide, water and nitric oxide
carbon dioxide, water and nitrogen dioxide

questions.solution_md: C + 4HNO₃ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 4NO₂ — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Copper turnings are warmed with nitric acid diluted 1 : 1 with water. A colourless gas forms inside the tube, but reddish-brown fumes appear at its mouth. The colourless gas is:
questions.solution_md: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO; at the mouth 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Sulphur powder is heated with concentrated nitric acid. The sulphur is converted into:
questions.solution_md: S + 6HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 6NO₂ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the reaction 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO, how many of the eight nitric acid molecules act as an oxidising agent (that is, have their nitrogen changed into nitric oxide)?
questions.solution_md: Only 2 nitrogen atoms end up in NO; the other 6 stay as nitrate ions in 3Cu(NO₃)₂ and act only as an acid — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Reddish-brown fumes appear at the mouth of a test tube in which copper is reacting with dilute nitric acid.

**Reason (R):** The nitric oxide formed in the tube combines with oxygen of the air to form nitrogen dioxide.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A: 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂ — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Copper gives hydrogen gas with concentrated nitric acid.

**Reason (R):** Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: A is false: copper gives nitrogen dioxide, not hydrogen. R is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of copper with concentrated nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the action of hot concentrated nitric acid on charcoal.

answer.model_answer_md: C + 4HNO₃ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 4NO₂.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the oxidation of sulphur by hot concentrated nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: S + 6HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 6NO₂.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: State one observation when concentrated nitric acid is added to copper turnings.

answer.model_answer_md: Reddish-brown fumes are given off (or: the copper dissolves and the solution turns green, then blue on dilution).

questions.solution_md: Brown fumes.

questions.stem_md: Copper turnings weighing 12.7 g dissolve completely in excess concentrated nitric acid. What volume of nitrogen dioxide, measured at STP, is given off? Give the answer in litres. (Cu = 63.5; one mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L at STP)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{Cu + 4HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2H2O + 2NO2}$: one mole of copper gives two moles of nitrogen dioxide. Moles of Cu $= \dfrac{12.7}{63.5} = 0.2$. Moles of $\ce{NO2} = 2 \times 0.2 = 0.4$. Volume $= 0.4 \times 22.4 = 8.96$, so 8.96 L.

questions.stem_md: Copper weighing 9.525 g dissolves completely in dilute nitric acid. What volume of nitric oxide, measured at STP, is formed? Give the answer in litres. (Cu = 63.5; one mole of a gas occupies 22.4 L at STP)
questions.solution_md: $\ce{3Cu + 8HNO3 -> 3Cu(NO3)2 + 4H2O + 2NO}$: three moles of copper give two moles of nitric oxide. Moles of Cu $= \dfrac{9.525}{63.5} = 0.15$. Moles of NO $= 0.15 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 0.1$. Volume $= 0.1 \times 22.4 = 2.24$, so 2.24 L.

questions.stem_md: Compare the action of concentrated and dilute nitric acid on copper by writing the balanced equation for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Concentrated: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂ (reddish-brown gas). Dilute: 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO (colourless gas).

questions.solution_md: Two equations.

questions.stem_md: Hot concentrated nitric acid is added separately to charcoal and to sulphur. (a) Write a balanced equation for each reaction. (b) Name the gas given off in both, and state its colour. (c) Which property of nitric acid do both reactions show? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) C + 4HNO₃ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 4NO₂; S + 6HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 6NO₂. (b) Nitrogen dioxide, reddish brown. (c) Nitric acid acts as an oxidising agent: it gives oxygen that oxidises carbon to carbon dioxide and sulphur to sulphuric acid, and is itself reduced to NO₂.

questions.solution_md: Equations; NO₂; oxidising agent.

questions.stem_md: A clean magnesium ribbon is dropped into very dilute nitric acid (about 1%). The gas given off is:
questions.solution_md: Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂: very dilute acid gives hydrogen with magnesium — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Nitric acid forms only one kind of salt, sodium nitrate, with sodium hydroxide. This shows that nitric acid is:
questions.solution_md: One replaceable hydrogen per molecule, so only normal salts (nitrates) form — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Dilute nitric acid is added to sodium hydrogen sulphite. The gas given off, and a test for it, are:

options.text_md: carbon dioxide, which turns lime water milky
hydrogen sulphide, which turns lead acetate paper black
sulphur dioxide, which turns orange acidified potassium dichromate solution green
hydrogen, which burns with a pop

questions.solution_md: NaHSO₃ + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O + SO₂ — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Black copper(II) oxide is warmed with dilute nitric acid. The observation is:

options.text_md: the black solid dissolves to give a blue solution

questions.solution_md: CuO + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O; copper(II) nitrate solution is blue — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Iron filings give hydrogen with moderately dilute nitric acid just as they do with dilute hydrochloric acid.
questions.solution_md: False: nitric acid oxidises the hydrogen to water; only very dilute nitric acid gives hydrogen, and only with magnesium or manganese.

questions.stem_md: Besides magnesium, the metal ___ gives hydrogen with very dilute nitric acid.
questions.solution_md: **Manganese**: Mn + 2HNO₃ → Mn(NO₃)₂ + H₂.

questions.stem_md: Name the two metals that give hydrogen with very dilute nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: Magnesium and manganese.

questions.solution_md: Mg and Mn.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with dilute nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: ZnO + 2HNO₃ → Zn(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the action of dilute nitric acid on potassium hydrogencarbonate.

answer.model_answer_md: KHCO₃ + HNO₃ → KNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Write the balanced equation for the neutralisation of sodium hydroxide solution by dilute nitric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: NaOH + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O.

questions.solution_md: Equation.

questions.stem_md: Explain why only very dilute nitric acid gives hydrogen with metals, and write the balanced equation for its reaction with manganese.

answer.model_answer_md: Nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent, so it normally oxidises any hydrogen formed to water. In very dilute acid (about 1%) its oxidising power is weak, and with very reactive metals such as magnesium and manganese some hydrogen escapes. Mn + 2HNO₃ → Mn(NO₃)₂ + H₂.

questions.solution_md: Oxidising power; equation.

questions.stem_md: How would you distinguish dilute nitric acid from dilute hydrochloric acid using copper turnings? State the observation for each.

answer.model_answer_md: Warm each acid with copper turnings. Dilute nitric acid reacts: the solution turns blue and a colourless gas forms that turns reddish brown at the mouth of the tube (NO, then NO₂). Dilute hydrochloric acid does not react with copper: no change.

questions.solution_md: Copper reacts only with nitric acid.

marking_scheme.step: Nitric acid: blue solution and brown fumes at the mouth

questions.stem_md: In the brown ring test for a nitrate, the test solution is first mixed with:

options.text_md: copper(II) sulphate solution, before dilute hydrochloric acid is added
iron(III) chloride solution, before sodium hydroxide is added
silver nitrate solution, before dilute nitric acid is added
freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution, before concentrated sulphuric acid is poured down the side

questions.solution_md: Fresh FeSO₄ solution, then concentrated H₂SO₄ layered underneath; the brown ring forms at the junction — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A colourless liquid is warmed with copper turnings and gives reddish-brown fumes and a bluish-green solution. The liquid is most likely:
questions.solution_md: Only nitric acid oxidises copper with brown NO₂ fumes — option (b).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In the brown ring test, the brown ring forms at the top surface of the liquid in the test tube.
questions.solution_md: False: it forms at the junction of the heavy sulphuric acid layer and the upper layer of test solution and iron(II) sulphate.

questions.stem_md: In the brown ring test, why is concentrated sulphuric acid poured slowly down the side of the test tube?

answer.model_answer_md: So that the heavy acid sinks to form a separate layer below the solution, and the brown ring forms at the junction of the two layers.

questions.solution_md: Forms a separate lower layer.

marking_scheme.step: Separate layer, ring at the junction

questions.stem_md: A colourless liquid X turns blue litmus red. When warmed with copper turnings it gives reddish-brown fumes; with sodium carbonate it effervesces; and it gives a brown ring in the brown ring test. (a) Identify X. (b) Write the balanced equation for its reaction with sodium carbonate. (c) Name the gas given off with copper and write the balanced equation.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Concentrated nitric acid. (b) Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. (c) Nitrogen dioxide: Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂.

questions.solution_md: Acid; brown fumes with copper and a brown ring: nitric acid.

Complete each sentence by choosing the correct word from the bracket.

(a) In Ostwald’s process, ammonia is oxidised over a ___ (platinum / iron) gauze.

(b) Nitric oxide is a ___ (colourless / reddish-brown) gas.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the two reactants used to prepare nitric acid in the laboratory, and write the balanced equation. [2]

(b) Explain why (i) the apparatus is made entirely of glass and (ii) the receiver is cooled. [2]

(c) Give three reasons why the reaction mixture is not heated above 200 °C. [3]

(d) Calculate (i) the mass of potassium nitrate needed to prepare 25.2 g of nitric acid and (ii) the mass of potassium hydrogen sulphate formed at the same time. (K = 39, N = 14, O = 16, H = 1, S = 32) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Potassium nitrate and concentrated sulphuric acid. KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃.

(b) (i) Nitric acid vapour attacks cork and rubber. (ii) To condense the nitric acid vapour into a liquid.

(c) Nitric acid would decompose; the glass retort could crack; a hard crust of potassium sulphate would form (any three, with wasted fuel also accepted).

(d) One mole of nitric acid needs one mole of potassium nitrate and gives one mole of potassium hydrogen sulphate. Moles of nitric acid $= \dfrac{25.2}{63} = 0.4$. (i) Mass of potassium nitrate $= 0.4 \times 101 = 40.4$, that is 40.4 g. (ii) Molar mass of potassium hydrogen sulphate $= 39 + 1 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 136$; mass $= 0.4 \times 136 = 54.4$, that is 54.4 g.

questions.solution_md: Reactants and equation; reasons; three reasons; 1 : 1 : 1 mole ratio.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Write the balanced equation for the first step of Ostwald’s process and state the catalyst and temperature. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equations for the second and third steps. [2]

(c) (i) Why does the catalyst stay red-hot once the reaction has started? (ii) Why does concentrated nitric acid often look yellow? (iii) How can this colour be removed? [3]

(d) Calculate the volumes, at STP, of (i) oxygen needed and (ii) nitric oxide formed when 8.5 g of ammonia is oxidised in the first step. (N = 14, H = 1; molar volume 22.4 L) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O; platinum gauze, about 800 °C.

(b) 2NO + O₂ → 2NO₂; 4NO₂ + 2H₂O + O₂ → 4HNO₃.

(c) (i) The oxidation of ammonia is exothermic; the heat given out keeps the gauze hot. (ii) Some acid decomposes, and the nitrogen dioxide formed dissolves in it. (iii) Bubble dry air (or carbon dioxide) through the warm acid, or add water.

(d) Moles of ammonia $= \dfrac{8.5}{17} = 0.5$. From the equation, 4 moles of ammonia need 5 moles of oxygen and give 4 moles of nitric oxide. (i) Moles of oxygen $= 0.5 \times \dfrac{5}{4} = 0.625$; volume $= 0.625 \times 22.4 = 14$, that is 14 L. (ii) Moles of nitric oxide $= 0.5$; volume $= 0.5 \times 22.4 = 11.2$, that is 11.2 L.

questions.solution_md: Equations with conditions; reasons; 4 : 5 : 4 mole ratio.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain why nitric acid acts as an oxidising agent, and name the gas formed from the acid when (i) concentrated and (ii) dilute nitric acid reacts with copper. [2]

(b) Write the balanced equations for the reaction of copper with (i) concentrated and (ii) dilute nitric acid. [2]

(c) Write the balanced equations for the action of hot concentrated nitric acid on (i) carbon and (ii) sulphur, and state one observation common to both. [3]

(d) 19.05 g of copper dissolves completely in dilute nitric acid. Calculate (i) the volume of nitric oxide formed at STP and (ii) the mass of copper(II) nitrate formed. (Cu = 63.5, N = 14, O = 16; molar volume 22.4 L) [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) It decomposes easily to give oxygen, which oxidises other substances. (i) Nitrogen dioxide. (ii) Nitric oxide.

(b) (i) Cu + 4HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O + 2NO₂. (ii) 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO.

(c) (i) C + 4HNO₃ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + 4NO₂. (ii) S + 6HNO₃ → H₂SO₄ + 2H₂O + 6NO₂. Reddish-brown fumes are given off in both.

(d) Moles of copper $= \dfrac{19.05}{63.5} = 0.3$. Three moles of copper give two moles of nitric oxide and three moles of copper(II) nitrate. (i) Moles of nitric oxide $= 0.3 \times \dfrac{2}{3} = 0.2$; volume $= 0.2 \times 22.4 = 4.48$, that is 4.48 L. (ii) Molar mass of copper(II) nitrate $= 63.5 + 2 \times 14 + 6 \times 16 = 187.5$; mass $= 0.3 \times 187.5 = 56.25$, that is 56.25 g.

questions.solution_md: Oxygen from decomposition; two copper equations; carbon and sulphur; 3 : 2 and 1 : 1 ratios.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by saying that nitric acid is monobasic? Name the normal salt it forms with potassium hydroxide. [2]

(b) A magnesium ribbon is placed in very dilute nitric acid. Write the balanced equation, and explain why more concentrated nitric acid does not give this gas. [2]

(c) Write the balanced equations for the reactions of dilute nitric acid with (i) copper(II) oxide, (ii) sodium carbonate and (iii) sodium hydrogen sulphite. [3]

(d) Dilute nitric acid is added to three test tubes holding sodium hydrogencarbonate, sodium sulphite and copper(II) oxide. State one observation for each tube, naming any gas given off. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Each molecule has one replaceable hydrogen atom, so it forms only one kind of salt (a normal salt). Potassium nitrate, KNO₃.

(b) Mg + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂. More concentrated nitric acid is a strong oxidising agent and oxidises the hydrogen to water.

(c) (i) CuO + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O. (ii) Na₂CO₃ + 2HNO₃ → 2NaNO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. (iii) NaHSO₃ + HNO₃ → NaNO₃ + H₂O + SO₂.

(d) Sodium hydrogencarbonate: brisk effervescence of carbon dioxide (turns lime water milky). Sodium sulphite: effervescence of sulphur dioxide, with a smell of burning sulphur (turns acidified potassium dichromate green). Copper(II) oxide: the black solid dissolves to a blue solution; no gas.

questions.solution_md: Basicity; hydrogen only from very dilute acid; three equations; three observations.

questions.stem_md:
Three unlabelled bottles, P, Q and R, contain dilute nitric acid, dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulphuric acid, in some order.

(a) Copper turnings are warmed with a sample from each bottle. Only the sample from P reacts. Identify P, state two observations and write the balanced equation. [3]

(b) Describe how the brown ring test is carried out on a sample from P, and state where the brown ring appears. [3]

(c) Suggest one reagent that distinguishes Q from R. State the observation with each acid, and write the balanced equation for the reaction that gives a visible change. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) P is dilute nitric acid. The solution turns blue, and a colourless gas forms that turns reddish brown at the mouth of the tube. 3Cu + 8HNO₃ → 3Cu(NO₃)₂ + 4H₂O + 2NO.

(b) Mix the sample with freshly prepared iron(II) sulphate solution in a test tube. Tilt the tube and pour concentrated sulphuric acid slowly down the side so that it forms a separate layer at the bottom. A brown ring appears at the junction of the two layers.

(c) Barium chloride solution. Dilute sulphuric acid gives a white precipitate of barium sulphate (insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid); dilute hydrochloric acid gives no precipitate. H₂SO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄ + 2HCl. (Silver nitrate is also accepted: a curdy white precipitate with hydrochloric acid only.)

questions.solution_md: Copper reacts only with nitric acid; brown ring procedure; barium chloride for sulphate.
